name: tailcat
desc: Netcat-like tool over Tailscale's data plane, without its control plane
why: Netcat-style pipes over Tailscale's WireGuard data plane, minus the control plane, is a revealing look at how the overlay actually moves packets.

brief.what_it_is: Tailcat is a netcat-style command-line tool and Go library that pipes data between two machines over an encrypted Tailscale-style tunnel, without needing a Tailscale account or the Tailscale control plane. One side runs a server (listener) that prints a short tailcat address, and the other side passes that address to the client. Data in and out is ordinary stdin/stdout, TCP port forwarding, SOCKS5, SSH, SFTP, file drop boxes, or a throughput test, depending on the service chosen. Traffic is WireGuard-encrypted end to end, bootstrapped through a DERP relay, and upgraded to a direct UDP path when NAT traversal succeeds.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as Tailscale's data plane without its control plane: point-to-point WireGuard tunnels between two machines, with connection metadata exchanged out of band however you like. It also describes itself as "Tailscale without Tailscale, by Tailscale".
brief.how_it_works: The server generates a WireGuard keypair (and by default a pre-shared key) and encodes them, plus DERP region info, into a tailcat address (a "tc" prefix followed by base64 CBOR). The client parses that address, connects to the same DERP relay, and sends a "Meow" discovery message; the server adds it as a WireGuard peer, and the WireGuard handshake runs over DERP at first while magicsock hole-punches toward a direct UDP path. The userspace stack uses WireGuard, magicsock, and gVisor netstack, so no TUN device, routes, DNS changes, or root access are needed.

commands_seen.context: Starts a server (listener). It prints a selected bootstrap relay region and a line like '🐈 Server listening with new address: tc...', then waits for a client.
Client side: pipes stdin into the tailcat address given as the argument; the server's stdout receives 'hello'.
Serves local TCP ports 8080 and 8443 through the tunnel (the README also lists 'tailcat serve all').
Client side: makes the server's port 8080 appear on local port 18080 and the server's port 3306 on local port 3306.
Runs an SSH server that accepts keys from a local authorized_keys file (other sources, including user@github, can be comma-separated).
Runs an SSH server with no client authentication, so the tailcat address itself is the credential. The README warns strongly against sharing it publicly.
Runs a write-only drop box that receives files into ~/inbox; senders share the printed tailcat address.
Sender side: copies a file to the drop box by running the system scp with the connection routed through tailcat.
Client side: runs an iperf-like throughput and latency test against a server started with 'tailcat serve perf'. It refuses to run through a shared DERP relay unless --via-derp is given.
Pings the server and keeps trying until a direct (non-DERP) path works, exiting non-zero if none does.
Generates a saved key named 'default' pinned to the nyc region, so the server address stays stable across restarts.

brief.install_notes: Prebuilt static binaries are listed for Linux and Windows, .deb and .rpm packages, Homebrew (macOS), Scoop (Windows), Snap, a container image, Nix (Linux and macOS), AUR (Arch), and conda-forge (Linux, macOS, Windows). FreeBSD and OpenBSD are only covered by building from source with the Go toolchain, as is the js/wasm browser build. The README points to INSTALL.md for details, which I did not fetch. No Tailscale account, root or admin access, or configuration is needed. By default it uses Tailscale's free rate-limited DERP relays via the derpmap at https://tailcat.dev/derpmap.json, and you can run your own derper with a hostname and TLS certificate.
brief.standout: It reuses Tailscale's WireGuard, magicsock, and gVisor netstack as a userspace library, so you get NAT traversal and encryption without a TUN device or root, and the address itself carries a WireGuard pre-shared key. The README also has a neat safety feature: 'tailcat ssh' probes DNS-named destinations as a stranger would and refuses to connect if the SSH server accepts that login.
brief.status: unknown. The README gives no version number, release date, or last commit date. The History section says it was open-sourced in August 2026 at the TailscaleUp conference, and it describes recent work (a refactor into a regular Go module client, and open issues such as #4 and #7). The README also says there are no API or CLI stability promises, so it is clearly actively developed but not a stable release.
brief.caveats: No API, CLI, or wire-format stability promises. The public DERP relays have no uptime SLA or throughput targets and may be revoked at any time. The web demo is experimental and browser traffic goes over DERP only, with no direct connections until WebRTC support lands (issue #4). no-auth-ssh makes the address a full shell credential, so it must not be published in DNS. Addresses published in DNS TXT records need --allow or --ssh-authorized-keys. Compression is not used for transfers. The perf command refuses to run through Tailscale's shared relays. Installation is uneven: no macOS static binary, and FreeBSD and OpenBSD require building from source. The README does not give a license, and I did not check one.
quotes: You don't need a Tailscale account, root/admin access on the machine (it doesn't alter your machine's routing tables, DNS, etc.). It's just a userspace library and CLI tool.
Who needs port forwarding or port knocking?
fetch_log: https://github.com/tailscale/tailcat (homepage, GitHub repo): fetched successfully; README returned. Its linked INSTALL.md, SECURITY.md, and docs were not fetched; the brief is based on the README alone.

judge.reason: It exposes Tailscale’s normally hidden WireGuard and NAT-traversal data plane as a no-account, no-root pipe, making overlay networking tangible.

entry.title: tailcat
entry.tldr: A netcat that tunnels over Tailscale's WireGuard data plane with no account, no root and no setup, just a short address you hand to the other side.
entry.deeper_look:
Tailcat connects two machines with an encrypted tunnel and then lets you pipe things through it. Run `tailcat` on one machine and it prints an address starting with `tc`. Hand that address to the other machine and you can send stdin, forward TCP ports, run an SSH or SFTP server, drop files into an inbox, or measure throughput. The README's own tagline is "Tailscale without Tailscale, by Tailscale".

The address is the interesting part. It encodes a WireGuard keypair, by default a pre-shared key, and the region of a DERP relay, all as base64 CBOR. The client connects to the same relay and sends a discovery message, and the server adds it as a WireGuard peer. The handshake first runs through the relay while the tool hole-punches toward a direct UDP path. If that works, traffic leaves the relay entirely.

It does this as a userspace library, built on WireGuard, magicsock and gVisor's netstack. That means no TUN device, no routing table changes, no DNS changes and no root. It is also a Go library, so the same machinery can be embedded in other programs.

The underlying idea is the split between a control plane, which decides who may talk to whom, and a data plane, which moves the packets. Tailcat keeps only the data plane and lets you pass the connection details around however you like. Using it is a good way to see how NAT traversal and relay fallback work in practice.

try_this.what_happens: Starts a listener, picks a relay region, and prints a line like 'Server listening with new address: tc...'. Whatever a client sends appears on its stdout.
On a second machine, pipes 'hello' to the address printed by the server (use your own address in place of the placeholder). The server's stdout receives it.
Pings the server and keeps trying until the path upgrades from the DERP relay to a direct UDP connection. Exits non-zero if it never does.

entry.whats_unique: It reuses Tailscale's own WireGuard, magicsock and netstack code as a userspace tool, so you get NAT traversal and encryption without an account or root. The address itself carries the keys.
entry.caveats: The README promises no stability for the CLI, API or wire format, and the public DERP relays have no uptime guarantee and could be withdrawn.
